founded.what: The year the house dates itself from, founded at Reims by a woman of the Henriot family, by its own account.

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: it buys grapes beyond its own vines and makes the wine itself, under its own name at Reims.

story: Henriot dates itself from 1808, when, by its own account, a woman of the Henriot family founded the house at Reims on vines in the Grand Cru villages of Verzy, Verzenay and Mailly-Champagne. In 1880 a marriage brought vines in Avize, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger and Chouilly, in the Côte des Blancs, and the house came to speak of six founding Grands Crus. The figure of the modern house is Joseph Henriot (1936 to 2015). He ran Charles Heidsieck from the middle of the 1970s until its sale in 1985, then traded the Henriot house and its vineyards for a share in Veuve Clicquot, which he led until 1994. That year he bought the Henriot name back, without the vineyards, and in 1995 and 1998 added Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune and William Fèvre in Chablis. The house's prestige cuvée was long Cuvée des Enchanteleurs; with the 2005 vintage it gave way to Cuvée Hemera, from the six crus in equal parts of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. In 2022 the family's group joined Artémis Domaines, and in the autumn of 2023 Terroirs et Vignerons de Champagne, the co-operative group of Nicolas Feuillatte, completed its purchase of Champagne Henriot. With the 2015 vintage the house gave its prestige wine the old name back, Cuvée des Enchanteleurs.

style.line: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from Grand Cru villages on both sides of Reims, long aged and dry: the Montagne de Reims vines of the founding and the Côte des Blancs vines a marriage brought in 1880, by the house's account.
style.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir lead: the Pinot Noir from Verzy, Verzenay and Mailly-Champagne, the Chardonnay from Avize, Chouilly and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, the six crus the house calls its founding Grands Crus.
style.reserve: Brut Souverain, the house's historic cuvée, is a blend of crus and of years, by the house.
style.lees: Long: more than ten years in the cellars for its prestige cuvée, by the house's sheets for Hemera 2013 and Cuvée des Enchanteleurs 2015.
style.dosage: Low: 3.5 grams a litre for Hemera 2013 and 2.5 for Cuvée des Enchanteleurs 2015, by the house.

nv.name: Brut Souverain
nv.note: The non vintage Brut, which the house calls its historic cuvée: a blend of several crus and several years.

cuvee.name: Cuvée Hemera

first.what: The first vintage, with which Hemera took the place of Cuvée des Enchanteleurs at the head of the house's range.

cuvee.rhythm: Made in the vintages the house chose: the 2005, 2006, 2008 and 2013 were sold as Hemera, and with the 2015 the same wine took back the name Cuvée des Enchanteleurs, by the house.
cuvee.blend: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in equal parts, by the house and the launch reports; no Meunier.
cuvee.sites: Six Grand Cru villages: Avize, Chouilly and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger in the Côte des Blancs for the Chardonnay, and Mailly-Champagne, Verzenay and Verzy on the Montagne de Reims for the Pinot Noir.
cuvee.making: A blend of the six crus alone, every component Grand Cru by the house's sheet for the 2013. The wine rests for years in the Reims cellars before release: the 2005 had twelve years on its lees and a dosage of 5 grams a litre by Decanter's launch report, and the 2013 at least ten years and 3.5 grams a litre by the house.
cuvee.lees: At least ten years in the cellars by the house's sheet for the 2013; twelve years for the 2005.
cuvee.young: Wheat toast and smoke over dried white blossom, with a sea spray note of iodine, as the house's notes on its second vintage describe it.
cuvee.aged: No note of a bottle kept long after release was sourced; the house's notes on the 2015, after more than ten years in its cellars, give candied lemon peel and acacia honey with a long finish.
cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

also.name: Cuvée des Enchanteleurs

first.what: Its first vintage was not found; the house's library sheets reach back to the 1977 vintage.

also.note: The older name of Henriot's prestige cuvée, sold in vintages such as 1977, 1988, 1996 and 1998 and set aside when Hemera began with the 2005 vintage. The house has since given it back: with the 2015 vintage the wine that was Hemera took its historic name again, from the same six Grand Cru villages in equal parts of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. The house makes it only in years it judges exceptional, by its own page. Keep both names: the vintage tells you which the label prints.
also.line: Cuvée des Enchanteleurs is the older Henriot name, set aside for Hemera in 2005 and restored by the house with the 2015 vintage.

table.house45: Henriot dates itself from 1808, at Reims. Its wines come from Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in six Grand Cru villages on both sides of the city, which it calls its founding crus. The name people in the trade remember is Joseph Henriot, who ran Veuve Clicquot and in 1994 bought his family's name back. The style is long aged and very dry, with years in the cellar before a bottle is sold. Brut Souverain is the bottle a guest usually meets. The prestige cuvée is Hemera, first made in 2005, and with the 2015 vintage the house gave it back its older name, Cuvée des Enchanteleurs.
table.house10: Henriot is the Reims house of 1808 whose wines come from six Grand Cru villages, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in balance.
table.cuvee45: Cuvée Hemera began with the 2005 vintage as Henriot's prestige Champagne. It is Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in equal parts, from six Grand Cru villages, three in the Côte des Blancs and three on the Montagne de Reims. It waits at least ten years in the cellar before it is sold. There is wheat toast, smoke and dried white blossom in the glass. With the 2015 vintage the house gave the same wine its older name, Cuvée des Enchanteleurs. I pour it at about nine degrees in a white wine glass, so the depth can open.
table.sale: Henriot's Hemera waited ten years and more in the cellar, and it comes from six Grand Cru villages alone. May I suggest a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: Hemera is Henriot's prestige vintage Champagne: equal Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from six Grand Cru villages, aged over ten years.
table.cuvee20: Henriot first made Hemera in 2005, a vintage of equal parts Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from six Grand Cru villages. With the 2015 vintage it took back its older name, Cuvée des Enchanteleurs.

guests.q: Is Hemera the same wine as Cuvée des Enchanteleurs?
guests.a: They are one line under two names. Enchanteleurs was the older prestige cuvée, Hemera took its place from the 2005 vintage, and with the 2015 vintage the house restored the name Enchanteleurs.
Yes. It is the wine of one harvest, made only in years the house chooses: Hemera 2005, 2006, 2008 and 2013, then the 2015 under the older name.
No, it is very dry: the house added 3.5 grams of sugar a litre to Hemera 2013 and 2.5 to the 2015 Enchanteleurs.

guests.q: Has Henriot anything to do with Veuve Clicquot?
guests.a: Only through history: Joseph Henriot traded his family's house for a share in Veuve Clicquot, led it until 1994 and then bought the Henriot name back.

traps: The class sheet prints Cuvée des Enchanteleurs/Hemera: Hemera is the name from the 2005 vintage to the 2013, and the house restored Cuvée des Enchanteleurs with the 2015, so each name is right for its vintages.
Henriot is not one of the three Heidsiecks: Joseph Henriot ran Charles Heidsieck until its sale in 1985, but the two houses are separate.
Hemera is a vintage wine of equal Chardonnay and Pinot Noir; Brut Souverain is the house's non vintage blend of crus and years.
Enchanteleurs is Henriot's; La Grande Dame is Veuve Clicquot's, the house Joseph Henriot once led, and the two are not to be swapped.

sheet.label: Cuvée Hemera; Cuvée des Enchanteleurs again from the 2015 vintage
sheet.note: The sheet prints both names, which are one line of wine: Cuvée des Enchanteleurs before the 2005 vintage, Cuvée Hemera from 2005 to 2013, and Cuvée des Enchanteleurs again from the 2015 vintage, by the house.

questions.q: Which prestige cuvée, first made in the 2005 vintage from six Grand Cru villages, is Henriot's?
questions.exp: Cuvée Hemera is Henriot's, made from the 2005 vintage and renamed Cuvée des Enchanteleurs with the 2015. Celebris is Gosset's, Grand Siècle is Laurent-Perrier's and Amour de Deutz is the Blanc de Blancs of Deutz.

questions.q: What did Joseph Henriot buy back in 1994?
opts: The Henriot name, without its vineyards
Bouchard Père et Fils in Beaune
questions.exp: He had traded the Henriot house and its vineyards for a share in Veuve Clicquot, and in 1994 bought the name back without the vines. He ran Charles Heidsieck until its sale in 1985 and added Bouchard Père et Fils in 1995.

questions.q: In what proportion do Chardonnay and Pinot Noir make Henriot's Cuvée Hemera?
questions.exp: Hemera is Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in equal parts, from three Côte des Blancs crus and three of the Montagne de Reims. A Chardonnay alone wine would be a Blanc de Blancs, and the blend holds no Meunier.

report: For the lead: the house's own page for Cuvée des Enchanteleurs 2015 says the wine that was Cuvée Hemera has taken back its historic name with the 2015 vintage (the Champagne Club's premiere and Gault and Millau agree), so the plan's standing of before is true of the old Enchanteleurs but not the whole story; the record teaches both and plan.json may want a ruling.
Henriot is not in the library and has no flagships record, so every fact rests on the house's pages or two secondary sources; no published Codex record is in tension.
The founder, Apolline Henriot by the house, is described and not named: her dates were not found; the 1880 marriage is told without the names because the spouses' dates were not found either.
Joseph Henriot (1936 to 2015): Wikipedia gives the years and Decanter his death on 27 April 2015 at 79; one Drinks Business profile gives 1942, which the record does not follow.

Joseph Henriot took over Charles Heidsieck in 1975 by one account and 1976 by others, and the trade of the Henriot house for a share in Veuve Clicquot is dated 1985 or 1987, so the record dates neither; the sale of Charles Heidsieck in 1985 and the buyback of the name without the vineyards in 1994 stand on several accounts.

Ownership: the 2022 merger into Artémis Domaines (Bloomberg, Decanter, The Drinks Business) and the October 2023 completion of the sale to Terroirs et Vignerons de Champagne (The Drinks Business, Just Drinks) are told as dated history; this touches the Nicolas Feuillatte record of chunk h4.

Left out for want of a source: the release year of Hemera 2005 (the plan's 2018 was not confirmed), the earlier names Cuvée Baccarat and Premier Cuvée (one account each), the first vintage of Enchanteleurs, and the meaning of either name, which no house page read gives; style.vessels and style.malolactic are empty because no house page read states them.
Gault and Millau's listing of the 2005 names Vertus and Oger beside the six crus; the house and Decanter give the six, which the record follows.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; the inference rests on the house buying back its name without its vineyards in 1994 and buying grapes since, and a refuter should read a label.

The young glass is the house's notes on the 2006 as a merchant prints them; the aged glass is the house's notes on the 2015, which spent over ten years in the cellars; no note of a bottle kept long after release was used.
The service temperature is the Codex's sparkling range of 8 to 10 degrees Celsius: the house's pages read gave none.
